Recipes: tuned backend settings, as data#

A setting that makes one model faster on one route can make another slower. For example, on the removed lean ROCm route 1024-token micro-batches sped up one MoE model's prompts by 3-8% and slowed the dense Qwen3.8-27B's by 4%. 1bit serve keeps such settings in config/recipes.json, not in code. Each recipe says what it matches, what it adds, why, and the measurement behind it:

{
  "id": "example",
  "match": {"device": ["hrx"], "drafter": ["dflash"]},
  "args": ["--spec-draft-p-min", "0.4"],
  "why": "what the setting does for this match",
  "measured": "the model, file, settings and numbers, measured with tools/bench.py",
  "source": "the PR that added it"
}

How serve applies them#

For each llama-server backend (hrx, cpu) serving a .gguf, serve checks every recipe against the launch:

match key Matches when
device the backend's device is in the list
architecture the file's general.architecture is in the list
moe the file has (true) or lacks (false) an <architecture>.expert_count above 0
drafter the drafter is in the list: none, mtp (--mtp) or dflash (--dflash)
gguf_keys every listed GGUF metadata key is present in the -m file (for example prism.hadamard.version, which PrismML's Hadamard-folded files carry and Qwen3.8 files do not)

A key that is left out matches anything. A matching recipe adds each flag in args, with the values after it, unless the backend's command line already has that flag. So whatever serve sets itself, including from the command line (--mtp-p-min, --mmproj's micro-batch), wins. It adds each variable in env unless it is already set. Serve prints what it added:

1bit serve: recipe example: --spec-draft-p-min 0.4
  • --recipes FILE replaces the built-in set with the recipes in FILE.
  • --no-recipes turns recipes off.
  • A malformed file (an unknown key, a recipe without measured) stops serve and names the problem.

tests/recipes_route.sh (ctest recipes_route) checks all of this without a GPU.

The built-in recipes#

Three, all on hrx for the qwen35 architecture, from the 2026-10-24/25 HRX drafter measurements (the Bonsai one is narrowed to PrismML's ternary files by a metadata key, below):

id matches adds measured
qwen35-dflash-p-min-0 hrx, qwen35, drafter dflash --spec-draft-p-min 0 56.6 / 30.8 / 20.6 tok/s code / prose / short with the Q8_0 drafter; a non-zero threshold cut prose to 22.5-23.3
bonsai-ternary-mtp-n2 hrx, qwen35, drafter mtp, prism.hadamard.version present --spec-draft-n-max 2 40.4 / 38.3 / 30.4 / 34.7 tok/s (code / prose / short / translation) against 41.7 / 36.8 / 27.2 / 33.2 at 3 drafts: the ternary files accept 0.76 of 2-token drafts, so short answers and translation win at 2 and only code wants 3-4
qwen35-mtp-max-3 hrx, qwen35, drafter mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 (what serve's --mtp-max 3 passes) 32.6 / 26.9 / 28.0 tok/s; acceptance falls to 0.17-0.60 past 7 drafts, so do not raise it

Both carry their full measured line in config/recipes.json. Older recipes were measured on build RFC #213 stage 3 removed: rotated-moe-ub1024 and rocm-dflash-p-min-0.4 (the lean ROCm build). New ones come with HRX measurements.

Recipes apply in file order. The first recipe to add a flag wins, so a narrower recipe goes before a broader one for the same flag.

Settings that follow from the files themselves stay in serve's code. Examples: the 2-bit decode copy a ternary Q4_0 file gets on HRX0, and the DFlash draft length, which is the drafter's dflash.block_size minus one.

Adding or changing a recipe#

Measure first, with tools/bench.py: the configuration with the setting against the one without it, in the same run. Put the numbers in measured and the PR in source. A recipe without a measurement does not load.
